newsitem.title: UK: SWIMMING-BANNED WORLD CHAMPION BACK IN THE FAST LANE.
newsitem.headline: SWIMMING-BANNED WORLD CHAMPION BACK IN THE FAST LANE.

text.p: World champion Lu Bin, a two-year doping ban behind her, resumed winning ways this week amid hopes that China's swimmers stay clear of drugs.
"It's good they're out there and swimming. Until there's a positive (test) you've got to assume they're okay," Australian head coach Don Talbot said after a World Cup meeting.
"We need them swimming there and if they're clean that's fine."

The Chinese are performing strongly on the World Cup circuit, leading three of the six women's categories, and Han Xue improved her own short-course world best in the 50 metres breaststroke on Wednesday.
Lu figured high in a Chinese women's team which swamped the opposition at the world long-course championships in Rome in September 1994 and bagged 12 of the 16 women's titles.
But a month later she was the most prominent of seven Chinese swimmers who tested positive at the Asian Games and, at the age of 17, she began a two-year ban from competition.
Western coaches and officials had long voiced doubts about the methods which had fuelled the astonishing advance of China's women swimmers from the late 1980s.
But, despite 19 positive dope tests, China has always denied systematic doping occurred along the lines employed by the former Communist regime in East Germany.

Lu is adamant drugs played no part in her successes -- 200 metres individual medley gold, two relay golds and 100 and 200 freestyle silvers at the 1994 world championships plus four golds and a 200 individual medley world record at the Asian Games which was subsequently annulled because of the positive test.
"One thing is for sure, I never took any drugs," she said after winning the 50 metres backstroke at the two-day Glasgow World Cup meeting, her first foray abroad since her ban.
"I'd like to show I have the ability to give a good performance in competition. I want to show I have something in my mind to keep training very hard for the last two years."
Gunnar Werner, honorary secretary of world swimming's governing body FINA, welcomed Lu's return and said she had undergone all the periodic dope tests the international federation had demanded.
"I met her in Beijing after the scandal and she said she'd do her best to get back again," Werner said. "We said 'good luck'...She's fulfilled all the requirements."
Werner said he did not know if any of the six other banned Chinese swimmers, including women's world 400 freestyle champion Yang Aihua, planned to return to competition.
"None of them said anything at the time and as far as I know they haven't requested a comeback," he said.
Lu said she had not considered quitting: "I never thought I would give up swimming. It was important to show my ability to be a top swimmer."
Tuesday's 50 backstroke victory was followed less happily on Wednesday by disqualification in the 100 backstroke for illegally kicking into the first turn.
But she is just feeling her way back into international competition, having previously raced only in the Beijing leg of the World Cup, and has yet to swim her speciality events.
One kilo lighter than before her ban, Lu trains 100 kilometres a week at the sports college in Beijing where she is studying.
Her 1994 times would have secured three gold medals at the 1996 Atlanta Olympics, with her annulled 200 individual medley world mark of 2:11.57 in a league of its own.
"I thought I could maybe have done that time in Atlanta. But for the future it is difficult," said Lu, wary of predicting too much for her comeback.
China pulled out of the 1995 World Cup series after the doping debacle and were snubbed by the Americans and Australians with a ban from that year's Pan-Pacific championships.
But the Chinese and former critics are now eager to build bridges of cooperation.

"A lot of countries have always been friendly and keep contact," Chinese coach Zhao Ge said, citing the cordial reception the swimmers received at a series of southern European meets in the summer of 1995 when they returned to international competition after the doping scandal.

Zhao said he and another Chinese coach visited the Australian Institute of Sport last November. Talbot says he will visit Beijing after the final World Cup meet in Paris in February to try to set up a series of youth swimming competitions.

"We want more relationships with other countries. A lot of coaches want friendship with China," said Zhao, coach of multi-world champion Liu Limin, who swam extremely fast times in the 100 and 200 butterfly in Glasgow.
"If we had more chance to go to America, that would be great. But it's so far from our country."
China's swimmers, some of them young and inexperienced, performed below expectation at the Atlanta Olympics and coach Zhao is not sure they can again achieve the domination of old.
"That is very difficult to say because in Australia and America the young swimmers are very good," he said. "We rely on ability and training hard," he said.
